paper.citation: J. Doe (2001), A Fictional Ordering Method. Fictional Journal 1:1-9.

background.question: How can unlabelled points be ordered along a path?
background.context: Earlier graph methods join near points, so a short edge across a gap can shortcut the path.

terms.meaning: each point joined to its k closest points

background.picture: Nine points are measured once each; nobody saw them move. We want the path they would lie on if they were steps of one process, so that the order along the path can be read off.
background.summary: The paper orders unlabelled points along a path. Its Introduction names one obstacle: in a plain k-nearest-neighbour graph a short edge across a gap joins two distant parts, and the shortest path then skips steps. It declares one change: keep the k nearest neighbours but make an edge longer than 1.0 cost more (the parameter boost).

primer.object: The method outputs an ordering of the points along a path: a line of points, each joined to the next by an edge.

parts.meaning: a joint between two points, drawn longer when the points are farther apart

primer.learn: which points come before which, and where a long edge marks a gap
